title: Probability of Independent and Dependent Events

lines:
In this lesson we will learn if one event affects another event and how to find its probability. But first try to answer this activity. 
Directions: State whether the result of the first event affects the result of the second event. 
\quad 1. Studying hard, getting a high grade 
\quad 2. Eating a lot, gaining weight 
\quad 3. Playing computer games, submitting all assignments and projects on time. 
\quad 4. Tossing a coin, rolling a die 
\quad 5. Attending a singing lesson, raining today 
Sometimes the result of one event affects the probability of the second event like numbers 1 to 3. However, tossing a coin does not affect rolling a die as well as attending a singing lesson does not affect the probability of raining or not. When a first event affects the probability of a second event, the events are said to be dependent, while when the first event does not affect the probability of the second, the events are independent.

Examples: 
1. Tell whether the events are independent or dependent. Explain. 
\quad a. You flip heads on one coin and tails on another coin. 
Answer: The outcome of flipping one coin does not affect the outcome of flipping the other coin. So, the events are independent. 
\quad b. Your teacher chooses one student to lead a group, and then chooses another student to lead another group. 
Answer: The teacher cannot pick the same student to lead both groups. So, there are fewer students to choose from when the leader of the second group is chosen. So, the events are dependent. 
\quad c. Select three cards, one at a time, from a standard poker deck. 
Answer: When you select a card for the first time you have 52 choices, but for the second time there will only be 51 left, then for the third time there will be 50 left and so the word one at a time indicates dependent events, because the first choice affects the second choice and so on. 
Let us consider problems that involve independent and dependent events

Two events are independent if the occurrence of one of the events gives no information about whether or not the other event will occur; that is the events have no influence on each other. If two events A and B, are independent, then the probability of both events occurring is the product of the probability of A and the probability of b. In symbols, P(A and B) = P(A) ∙ P(B). 
When the outcome of one event affects the outcome of another event, they are dependent events. If two events, A and B, are dependent, then the probability of both events occurring is the product of the probability of A and the probability of B after A occurs. In symbols, P(A and B) = P(A) ∙ P(B after A).
